extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels, corporate communicators, press-release writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations practitioners on analyzing clients and publics, creating ‘news’, selecting media, and designing messages that appeal to human instincts and group dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze client problem and objectives first
rubrics_metrics.description: First he must analyze his client’s problem and his client’s objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before designing any message or campaign, clearly define the client's goal(s). Use this analysis to guide message selection, tactics, and measures of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the public (audience) and its subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Then he must analyze the public he is trying to reach... visualize himself as member of many publics and their subdivisions (manufacturers, retailers, importers, employers, workers, financiers, politicians, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment the audience into meaningful groups (by occupation, geography, age, language, education, etc.) and imagine the issue from each subgroup's perspective to find influential appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise a plan of action and choose methods/media
rubrics_metrics.description: He must devise a plan of action for the client to follow and determine the methods and the organs of distribution available for reaching his public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate channels (press, moving pictures, lecture platform, advertising, direct mail, stage, radio, word of mouth, pulpit, schoolroom, legislative chamber) aligned with audience habits and campaign goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate interaction between client and public
rubrics_metrics.description: Finally he must try to estimate the interaction between the public he seeks to reach and his client. How will his client’s case strike the public mind?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how messages will be received, what associations audiences will make, and adjust tone/content to fit expected reactions and possible resistances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it easy for the public to pick the issue (use headlines/simplification)
rubrics_metrics.description: He must make it easy for the public to pick his issue out of the great mass of material; overcome the tendency of public attention to 'flicker' and 'relax.' The headline is a compact, vivid simplification of complicated issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise, vivid leads/headlines and visual cues (cartoons, symbols) to distill complex ideas into immediately graspable forms; avoid heavy abstractions in front-line messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify and dramatize abstract discussions and heavy facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract discussions and heavy facts are the groundwork... but they cannot be given to the public until they are simplified and dramatized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate technical or detailed information into dramatized, relatable events or images so broad audiences can understand and retain the message; reserve complexity for behind-the-scenes materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create news — make ideas newsworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel is a creator of news for whatever medium he chooses to transmit his ideas. He must lift startling facts from his whole subject and present them as news; isolate ideas and develop them into events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the most inherently interesting or surprising elements of a story and package them as timely news items, press events, or stunts so they gain placement in competitive news markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply truthful, accurate, verifiable news to the press
rubrics_metrics.description: To the newspaper the public relations counsel serves as a purveyor of news... it is because he acts as the purveyor of truthful, accurate and verifiable news to the press that the conscientious and successful counsel is looked upon with favor by the journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accuracy and verifiability to build trust with journalists; false or unverifiable 'news' undermines relations and credibility (ethical standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to fundamental instincts and emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal to the instincts and the universal desires is the basic method through which he produces his results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages that tap universal drives (self-preservation, hunger, sex, curiosity, pugnacity, self-display, parental love, gregariousness, individualism, acquisition, construction, play, habit, suggestion/imitation). Use concrete examples (home/radiator ads for shelter, food visuals for gustatory appeal, 'the skin you love to touch' for sex/beauty) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit self-preservation and safety appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The instinct of self-preservation... is most flexible. Examples: advertisements or campaigns that stress health/hygiene, iron-supplement slogan, insurance as safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appeals to health, safety, hygiene, and economic security; frame offerings or behaviors as protective measures to motivate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gustatory and sensual appeals where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers use graphic delineation of food and drink to appeal to gustatory sense (Gulden Mustard ad); soap and beauty products use sex appeal (Woodbury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In product or event promotion, use vivid sensory imagery to create desire; beware of taste/decency boundaries depending on audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ curiosity and wonder (suspense) to build interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity and wonder are continually employed. Statesmen and publishers send out 'feelers' or use suspense to arouse interest ('What is wrong with this picture?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teasers, pre-announcements, puzzles, or suspenseful hooks to build anticipation before a major announcement or release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage pugnacity/contest/spectacle to mobilize crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Pugnacity (anger/contest) is used in constructing events—staging battles against evils, announcing counts (e.g., tuberculosis campaigns), using warfare metaphors ('kill the germs', 'swat the fly'). Contests and issues attract attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame issues as conflicts or contests when appropriate (debates, challenges, competitions) to provoke involvement and tribal identification; recognize ethical/dangerous downsides (can suppress/oppress).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contests, tests, and issues to draw participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests and contests are continually devised; contests bring people together because of the element of conflict and identification with competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design contests or competitions (sales contests, consumer promotions) judged by credible panels to attract participation and publicity (example: 'Bring home the Beech-Nut' sales contest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use self-display/public recognition to strengthen commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-display-elation motive: public praise or visible recognition (naming rooms or beds after donors, elaborate letterheads) increases adherence and turns lukewarm supporters into active forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer public honors, naming opportunities, or status markers to convert passive supporters into advocates; public recognition reinforces commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilize group leaders and influencers to carry messages
rubrics_metrics.description: A group leader gains such power that his adherence to a cause brings others along. The public relations counsel enlists leaders (society leaders, political leaders, leaders by geography, age, language, education) to bring their followings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and recruit influential figures whose endorsement will cascade through their networks and affiliated groups; build cross-section committees (e.g., hotel anniversary committee with banker, society woman, lawyer, preacher) to create stereotype-based credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment by and exploit stereotypes and mental habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes and mental habits (stereotypes, clichés) are short-cuts to reactions; the counsel may use, combat, or create stereotypes (e.g., national symbols, Danube waltz for Austria, 'square deal' for Roosevelt); visible objects serve as stereotypes (flag, instruments, white buildings for cleanliness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use familiar stereotypes to anchor new ideas, consciously combat harmful stereotypes by reframing language/symbols, or create new memorable slogans/symbols; beware overuse which leads to shop-worn clichés and the danger that words substitute for acts (demagoguery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use play and spectacle for fundraising and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Play tendency: street fairs, fireworks, marble contests, horseshoe pitching provide outlets and help committees raise money or create civic goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, stage playful public events or spectacles to engage broad audiences and raise funds or awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit habit, imitation, and susceptibility to suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate tendencies include susceptibility to suggestion, imitation and habit; mental habits create stereotypes that aid quick responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage repeat exposure and ritualized behaviors to form habits; leverage imitation by showing peer adoption (social proof) to normalize desired actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectify human qualities with physical metaphors and visual symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Human qualities are best remembered by a physical sign; cartoons and metaphors (rock for courage, road for purpose) make abstract qualities concrete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong visual metaphors, icons, and cartoons in releases and campaigns to make abstract attributes instantly memorable and shareable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that 'news' criteria vary by outlet; timeliness alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: What is news for one newspaper may have no interest for another... timeliness is often important but not always sufficient for newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor pitches to the interests and definitions of newsworthiness of each outlet; beyond timeliness emphasize human interest, novelty, impact, conflict, prominence, or usefulness as fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallize obscure public tendencies before they express concretely
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief contribution is ability to understand and analyze obscure tendencies of the public mind and crystallize them before they reach definite expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor subtle shifts in public mood and create symbols/messages that articulate and mobilize latent sentiments early, thereby shaping the narrative rather than merely reacting.
